The decision worth defending is treating a transform's freshness differently from a topic's. The supervisor measures a message's age from when it arrived; a transform's age has to come from its own stamp, the time tf2 interpolates at, because a broadcaster can keep delivering the same old pose and every delivery would otherwise look fresh. We proved the split matters by stopping the relay and watching

subs.title: Inspect frames and commands with tf2 tools and RViz

c.v: By the end of this session, you have two drawings of the bench that came out of its own tools rather than out of memory: the frame tree, and the path a command takes from your terminal to the wheels.
installs an RViz configuration that shows the robot, its frames and its scan, and
node that reports the age of one transform and says when it has gone stale.
The two drawings describe the same robot, and a failure usually shows up in one of them only. The supervisor reads

and leaves the tree untouched, because the bridge publishes

items.v: Follow one command through the system. Every arrow below has a command that proves it, and none of them is a guess:

blocks.text:

items.v: Now separate the two pictures. Stop the relay in terminal 2 with Ctrl+C, and watch what changes and what doesn't:

blocks.text:
ros2 topic hz /odom        # nothing arrives any more
ros2 topic hz /tf          # unchanged
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo odom base_link     # still answers, with a fresh stamp

c.v: The supervisor logs that odometry is stale and the robot stops, while the frame tree carries on: the bridge publishes
travels through the relay. So a complete transform tree is no evidence that the bench's odometry path works, and the missing-input scenario later depends on exactly this split. Start the relay again.

items.v: Before writing the node, settle what "stale" means for a transform. The supervisor measures the age of a message from when it arrived, because a command's stamp can be zero or can come from a recording. A transform is different: its stamp is the time at which the pose was true, and it is the time tf2 interpolates at, so a transform that arrives again with an old stamp is old data however fresh its delivery is.
answers both questions; the difference is the time you hand it. This program feeds one copy the stamps and the other the arrivals:

blocks.text:
stamp 200 ms, arrived 220 ms: fresh by stamp true , by arrival true
stamp 250 ms, arrived 270 ms: fresh by stamp true , by arrival true
stamp 300 ms, arrived 320 ms: fresh by stamp true , by arrival true
stamp 300 ms, arrived 420 ms: fresh by stamp true , by arrival true
stamp 300 ms, arrived 520 ms: fresh by stamp true , by arrival true
stamp 300 ms, arrived 570 ms: fresh by stamp false, by arrival true
stamp 300 ms, arrived 620 ms: fresh by stamp false, by arrival true

c.v: to the end, because something keeps arriving. The stamp answer turns

at the 570 ms delivery, once the newest stamp is more than 250 ms old, and that 250 ms is the limit this watcher was given rather than anything tf2 decided. tf2 draws its own line much earlier, and that one is not a choice: a lookup at the current time extrapolates as soon as the current time is past the newest stamp (
). The first three deliveries are 20 ms behind the pose they carry, and the repeats of the 300 ms pose fall further and further behind it, so
Lookup would require extrapolation into the future
from the first delivery onwards, at 220 ms and at every row after it, while the watcher still calls the transform fresh until 570 ms. Two different questions, two different times. That is why

, which returns the newest transform whatever its age and never throws, and then judges the age against the limit you chose. A broadcaster that republishes an old pose is the case the frames topic listed as failing without an exception.
